Mr. Speaker, I rise to express my support for the motion so admirably presented by my colleague, the Hon. Barbara McDougall, Minister of State (Finance), and 1 share the enthusiasm with which she tabled this Bill.
It is high time the House legislated measures to counter the unfair and paralyzing effects of this regressive petroleum and gas revenue tax which has created considerable, and 1 may say regrettable, economic problems for Western Canada.
If we could turn back the clock, we would be delighted to do so, but we cannot. We do not have that power. We cannot compensate people for lost income nor for the psychological disruption produced in Western Canada. Nor can we resurrect lost business opportunities, but we can, however, create a climate conducive to economic recovery and investment growth.
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the Bill before the House today is to put the oil and gas industry back on the road to recovery, and to do so, it will make four major changes in the petroleum revenue taxation system.
These changes signify a clear recognition of the failure of this regressive tax introduced by the previous Government. The changes will eliminate the disastrous effects of attempts by the unfortunate previous Government to increase its revenue, in a highly questionable manner, by penalizing an industry and a region in this country that until then had been strong and dynamic.
The proposed changes are as follows:
-Gradually phase out the regressive tax on petroleum revenue by 1989;
-Provide welcome tax deductions for unused exploration and development expenditures;
-Exempt new oil and gas production and new oil and gas installations from the PGRT;
-Reduce cumbersome administrative procedures and accounting costs for thousands of Canadians who receive income from oil and gas wells, by allowing a basic deduction of $10,000;
Finally, eliminate the incremental oil revenue tax, as a stimulus for the successful entrepreneur.
Its confidence restored by the promise made by the Progressive Conservative Party to establish a more equitable tax system, in 1984 the petroleum and gas industry started on its difficult but nonetheless encouraging road to recovery.
Clear signs of this recovery have become increasingly frequent since the former National Energy Program was replaced by the Western Accord on March 28, 1985.
This growing activity is reflected in statistics on the number of active drilling platforms and the increasing number of oil and gas wells that will soon be in production.
During the first quarters of 1985, the utilization rate of petroleum and gas drilling platforms was 64 per cent, which is higher than it was during all four quarters of the last three years.
It is expected that a total of over 11,000 wells will be drilled in 1985, which means an increase of about 26 per cent over the record number reached in 1980, before the industry felt the negative impact of the National Energy Program which subsequently was to have such disastrous effects.
It is indeed a spectacular increase-almost double the number of wells drilled in 1982 at the peak of the disastrous energy program launched by the previous Government.
Unfortunately such statistics may well make some people yawn openly, but they do reflect encouraging employment prospects. These new figures are encouraging as well because industry is banking on the adoption of amendments proposed in this Bill and on incentive measures related to provincial royalties.
Since the memorable Western Accord was signed, many companies have said they intend to boost their investments.

November 19, 1985
Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act
Among others, Imperial Oil has announced investments of about $1 billion in 1985, not bad by Canadian standards.
Shell Oil recently unveiled capital investment projects of some $500 million for 1985, not to mention the $200 million earmarked for expanding its oil sands processing plant near Peace River, a project which entails over 900 person-years in direct employment and 1,800 person-years in related works. Mr. Speaker, that is the outcome of an election promise which has been honoured after we took office and which was our campaign rallying cry: jobs, jobs, jobs,
Canterra's capital investment budget for western Canada has gone up 34 per cent in 1985.
Nova Corporation will spend some $500 million to expand its natural gas pipeline network.
BP Canada will invest $450 million to beef up its Wolf Lake crude oil development project.
These are all private sector initiatives.
We could go on and on listing the many concrete projects which have been hatched as a result of the renewed confidence of Canadians in their oil and gas industry.
Mr. Speaker, it has become obvious that the oil and gas sector has at last regained confidence and that such brightening prospects have prompted other provincial Governments and private interests to make further investments.
Average Canadians can also be optimistic and confident, and higher consumer spending reflects their buoyant mood.
In the first half of 1985 Alberta consumers spent 10 per cent more than they did during the same period last year.
In British Columbia-a dynamic province which was hard hit by the latest recession-retail sales did rise by 7 per cent in the first seven months of this year as compared with the same period in 1984.
In Saskatchewan, where some of my cousins live, employment growth in the first half of 1985 was much stronger than the national average.
The amendments contained in this Bill will be the starting point of Western Canada's economic revival so that our energy industry as a whole will benefit. The economic fallout will also be felt in a number of other regions and sectors.
As my colleague said yesterday, Mr. Speaker, and as other Members on this side pointed out, this Bill will mark the end of an era of unfair and discriminatory taxes.
I therefore suggest that we give it quick passage to provide a healthy economic climate in the oil and gas industry and at least attempt to help those who have been hit so hard directly and indirectly by the taxes on oil revenues.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to add a very personal note to this nearly official speech and say that the constituency of LaSalle benefits directly from the increased growth of the Western Canada oil industry. Indeed, yesterday, in preparing my intervention for today, I made a survey of some of the industries in my constituency. I can tell you that no fewer than 12 industries will benefit directly from increased orders as the result of the economic recovery in Western Canada.
I believe that it is somewhat inaccurate to say that recovery in Western Canada is concentrated only in that region. In my opinion, our country is truly integrated and it was a real discovery for me to find-and maybe I learned this rather late-that Canada is truly integrated and that the East-West market still exists.
I therefore urge this assembly to give passage to this Bill which will do something to compensate for the misfortunes which have hit one region in our country and affected all Canada.

What I have described are the direct results of our new policy, and if we made the mistake of withdrawing this Bill now, the doors would close much more quickly than they opened.

To use the language of construction, Mr. Speaker, when you throw a bomb on a building, you cannot throw another bomb beside it to rebuild it. Reconstruction takes much longer. If one were sitting in Atlantic Canada listening to the Hon. Member, one would have to conclude that all those years of Liberal Government gratuities given to the part of Canada he represents, indeed to all of Canada, should have produced a great increase in employment and a strong surge in our economy. Indeed, if the Liberal approach of liberally taking money from private sector pockets and redistributing it to other parts of the country had worked, we would not have seen unemployment rise from one million people in 1980 to 1.5 million by the time that Government left office in 1984.
We agree that benefits were delivered to provinces and regions such as Cape Breton which the Hon. Member represents. However, if we were to plot on a graph the data regarding the transfer of funds to the Atlantic provinces under Liberal programs and the impact on unemployment and the health of the economy, the level of disposable income and the new economic initiatives by private interests in that region, we would find the results were inversely proportional to the assistance given. That is, the more money we pumped in by way of Liberal Government hand-outs, the more unemployment increased. As the Government in Ottawa mounted a
major war with the Atlantic provinces, particularly Newfoundland, unemployment continued to rise.
The Hon. Member asked us to show what improvements in the economy this Government has brought about in the 14 months it has been in office. Over the last 14 months, more than 300,000 jobs were created, bringing unemployment down to 1.1 million from 1.5 million under the Trudeau regime. That is the evidence that the private sector incentive driven approach is far superior to the Liberal approach of taking money from one region of Canada and handing it out holus-bolus in the form of grants to another region.
This Government does indeed take a new approach. It places the incentives in the hands of those who can take greatest advantage of them. That is the purpose of the $250 million of drilling incentives to be made available annually. This will ensure the pace of offshore drilling in his region, and ensure that the benefits are returned to the people of those regions through the private companies and individuals who will make such investments.
In conclusion, let me say that the Hon. Member tended to mislead this House when he implied that Members sitting on the Government side today did not resist vehemently the Draconian and confiscatory nature of the NEP. If he consults Hansard and the record of the debates on Bill C-48, the Canada Lands Act, if he would consult in particular the record of committee hearings in response to the budgetary measures flowing from the NEP, he would find indeed that members of this Government resisted most vocally not only the goals and objectives of the NEP, but the very divisive and impudent way in which it was foisted upon this country by the Government of which he was a part. I would ask the Hon. Member to clarify for the record that indeed it was the outspoken objection on the part of members of this Party that led to an unprecedented overthrow of a Government and its replacement with one which is devoted to creating a stronger economy and thousands and thousands of new jobs.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a considerable degree of relief that I can stand and support Bill C-82, an Act to amend the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act and the Income Tax Act. One of the most important items announced in the Western Accord last March was the elimination of the federal oil and gas taxes or charges, including the petroleum and gas revenue tax, the petroleum compensation charge and the Canadian ownership special charge together with the incremental oil revenue tax. Following the announcement by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in his May Budget, the legislation now before us will formally mark the elimination of both the PGRT and the IORT. No westerner who experienced the devastating effect of the National Energy Program, the most punitive measure of which was this PGRT that was imposed on January 1, 1981 for oil and natural gas production revenues and royalties, can underestimate the value of the steps now being taken in this respect.
Since the Western Accord was announced last March, and on a comparison of 1983 with 1985, drilling is up by 60 per cent, exploration and capital expenditures are up by 50 per cent and direct employment has created an additional 25,000 jobs.
The spinoffs in Alberta alone are significant. Employment in other industries has increased significantly. Retail sales have improved and real estate sales are up, with vacancy rates showing the first decline in some five years.
The current rate of PGRT is 16 per cent, with an effective rate of 12 per cent on conventional oil and gas and 8 per cent on synthetic oil, after the resource allowance, where applicable.
Under the terms of the Western Accord and this legislation, the PGRT will be totally eliminated by January 1, 1989. In addition, the PGRT will not apply to approved major new energy projects or to any new production of conventional oil, natural gas or natural gas liquids brought on stream after April 1, 1985. Under the schedule for phasing out, the rate of PGRT will be cut in half and will be totally eliminated by 1989.
The Government of Canada has agreed to reduce further the burden of PGRT on individuals by making the first $10,000 of income exempt from the tax. This will mean that an estimated two-thirds of those individuals who are currently paying PGRT will no longer be required to do so. The PGRT was perhaps the most bitterly criticized aspect of the National Energy Program. Being levied on revenues rather than profits or even cash flow, this tax was closely related to a federal royalty.
The tax also has been plagued by technical and administrative difficulties. The preceding Government subjected the
November 19, 1985

Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act to numerous amendments, many of which were not legislated until a considerable time after coming into effect. This left the industry in limbo. Our Government has stated that the PGRT would be removed and this commitment is being fulfilled.
No PGRT will be levied with respect to new production of oil, natural gas or gas liquids after March 31, 1985. New production has been defined to include production from new wells spudded after March 31, 1985, plus incremental production as a result of enhanced recovery schemes, including waterflood schemes commencing operation after March 31, 1985. New production will include production from new development wells on proven acreage but not production from currently shut-in wells that came on stream after March 31, 1985.
The federal and provincial Governments have agreed that the phase-out of the PGRT is necessary to stimulate reinvestment in Canadian exploration for the development and release of new oil and gas reserves. New exploration and development activity will potentially be rewarded by allowing non-taxable corporations to apply a portion of their newly incurred income tax write-offs, otherwise available as a credit, against their PGRT liability.
The Western Accord has provided the industry with strong incentives to explore and produce, which contrasts strongly with the policies in effect between 1973 and 1984. In general, those policies restricted Canadian resource development through various combinations of low oil prices, high taxes and restricted markets. There was a decline in Canadian spending in 1981 and 1982, in response to the National Energy Program, shut-in gas markets and other factors.
It became more apparent in 1984 that the Canadian energy policy had to be completely overhauled and petroleum industry expenditures came back strongly, in anticipation of this revised policy. It is anticipated that capital and development expenditures during 1985 will be some 20 per cent higher than last year and some 30 per cent higher than in 1983. Drilling activity in this country set an all time record last year, a record which this year's drilling has already surpassed. That 1984 record was based on anticipation that the Conservative Government would come through with its promises, as we have.
Now, with a realistic energy policy, with exploration at high levels and with a number of new oil sands projects under development, the outlook for the next few years is extremely good. While global expenditures are down drastically, expenditures are setting new records in Canada. Global drilling has undergone a decline, especially in the United States, while in Canada drilling is at record levels. Globally, there are surpluses of crude oil and many Third World producers are permitting their production capacity to decline. However, in Canada the industry is spending record amounts on projects and geological prospects which will increase crude oil production capacity over the next many years.
Although Canada has abundant resources, national and provincial energy policies effectively put a damper on their development from the 1970 to 1981-82 era. The policies
Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act during that era included excessive taxation, controlled prices and a great deal of political uncertainty. As a result, crude oil development, particularly during that period, was extremely constrained. However, the situation is greatly different today.
Because of our completely overhauled energy policy, our favourable resource base and our proximity to the United States oil and gas markets, the Canadian sector of the petroleum industry is likely to see continuing high levels of activity throughout the remainder of this decade. The Western Accord swept away artificial elements of Government-controlled and administered economics of the industry's production sector. It ushered in an era which will see further dramatic changes in the way the Canadian upstream sector operates and in the style in which it is managed.
Our Government recognized that the oil and gas industry could provide important national economic opportunities. Our energy resources can be produced and sold at internationally competitive prices. Canada's energy policy during the last decade prevented it from fully capitalizing on the development of its hydrocarbon resources. Governments at both the provincial and federal levels agreed that the federal Government should treat the petroleum industry like other industries, by taxing profits rather than revenues, and everyone applauds the demise of that most discriminatory petroleum and gas revenue tax over the next four years.
The special significance of the elimination of this tax is that it has already greatly improved the economics of oil and gas production. Since it is being eliminated over the next few years, the industry will experience annual improvements to cash flow as the tax burden is eased. With the acceptance of the principles of market pricing and the taxation of profits, the federal-provincial revenue sharing dispute has been settled. Disagreements based upon those particular issues were a major irritant and a source of uncertainty for the industry, and led to a full decade of political acrimony, during which time many opportunities were lost. At least this is all behind us now, Mr. Speaker.
Through the energy accords, this legislation, coupled with the frontier package and gas deregulation initiatives, the Canadian petroleum industry is likely to experience sustained high levels of activity, continuing good earnings and diversification into non-conventional resources. Unless there is a precipitous drop in oil prices, the future of this industry in this country is bright.
Our Government has recognized the dramatic shift in the public's perception of the Government and its policies. We have proclaimed our faith in the strengths and the virtues of the private sector. The current atmosphere is certainly more conducive to some form of rapport than it was even a year ago. We believe in a tripartite consultative process between Government, business and labour so that when public policy is formulated, the affected Parties have had an opportunity to express their views. We have lent an ear to what the business community has to say, and should the labour movement seek

November 19, 1985
Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act
the same access, 1 am confident it would meet the same reception. In my view, labour's participation is vital to any meaningful dialogue regarding public policy formulation.
Government ought to and is providing the framework within which the private sector is encouraged to get things done. Implicit in our oil policy is an attitude of trust and confidence in the private sector. We want to facilitate the private sector rather than regulate it. It is up to the private sector, as I said, to get on with the job.
Export of goods and services rose from 16 per cent to 18 per cent of the Gross National Product in the 1950s, to 20 per cent by the late 1960s, and now stands at 26 per cent. In effect, Mr. Speaker, Canada is more heavily dependent on world trade than any other industrialized nation. Yet, with a productivity performance up until now among the worst, we face increasing competition, not only from other industrialized nations but also from developing countries seeking to exploit their resources.
While faced with high-tech and resource competition abroad, Canada at home will have a rapidly aging population over the next 20 years and changing demand patterns that will cause major industrial restructuring and significant shifts in skill requirements in the labour force.
We face the necessity of decision times being reduced, and this means decentralization of decision responsibility to a much greater extent. It means less involvement of Governments in this process, and a greater reliance on the resource allocation properties of markets. A reduction in system rigidities caused by Government regulation and intervention is also a necessity.
Government programs, once in place, tend to be perpetuated and, I believe, a regular cost benefit review is required to ensure that resources available to Governments are being used most effectively.
Canada's budgetary deficits are a cause for overriding public concern, and the actions taken by our Government in restoring buoyancy to the energy industry are a palliative to that concern.
The need for an industrial strategy in Canada is not so much a call for a greater degree of Government involvement in the affairs of specific industries, but rather for a co-ordinated approach to an economic policy involving trade, taxation, competition, labour, research and development, industrial and stabilization policies. We have the policies in place to encourage the development of one of the world's most envied resource endowments.
Canada's geological potential is enormous. The western sedimentary basis, the source of most of Canada's conventional oil, has been drilled only one-tenth as much as similar regions in the United States. Our established resources are dwarfed by the potential of the oil sands, heavy oil and the frontiers.
Foreign investors have recognized the positive changes in Canada. In August, the Salomon Brothers of New York published a report that amounts to a ringing endorsement of Canada's new energy industry. The authors of that report said:
As a result of the overwhelmingly favourable policy changes that have occurred in Canada over the past year, the Canadian energy industry today has the opportunity to meet the challenges of domestic and world markets unfettered by onerous government regulation.
In an interview on Canadian radio, they said that Canada's geology offers great promise for future development and that investment prospects in Canada's oil industry are greater than in the United States, the United Kingdom, Norway and other areas around the world. By our energy policies, we now have access to energy markets. We have the technology to develop conventional and non-conventional sources. Above all, we have a revitalized oil and gas industry operating with confidence in a radically transformed policy environment.
In closing I want to point out that it has been one full year since this country voted overwhelmingly for a change. During the summer, 1984, the Progressive Conservative Party promised economic renewal and promised to create jobs.
Canada's resource sector has long been the bedrock of regional economic strength. In an effort to rebuild that vital sector and create hundreds of thousands of new jobs, the Progressive Conservative Government has been quick to take action. We have had the Atlantic Accord and the Western Accord, and two weeks ago the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) put forth the new terms for the Canada Petroleum Resources Act and the new policy for gas deregulation in Canada. All such steps are welcomed by Canadians from coast to coast. We are now clearly pursuing a path which will lead Canada to greater prosperity. Working together, we can build on the greatness of Canada for today and for the future.

maintopic: COMMISSION'S DECISION TO SECURE EVIDENCE IN SOVIET UNION
COMMISSION'S DECISION TO SECURE EVIDENCE IN SOVIET UNION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Justice Jules Deschenes has delivered his decision with regard to the taking of Soviet evidence. This decision falls far short of the expectations of many Canadians.
Presently the Soviet Union is engaged in a war in Afghanistan, a war the Soviet Union began as an invader in 1980. Since that time about 5,000 Soviet soldiers have been killed and an unknown larger number wounded. The Afghans have had their homeland ravaged and five million refugees have fled their homes. They have been uprooted by an invader that has the audacity to claim it was invited. These tactics are not unlike the tactics of Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union during the Second World War. There is no regard for the inviolability of borders, there is no regard for the population, and there is no regard for their own military forces.
It is ironic that the Deschenes Commission feels evidence can be gathered in the Soviet Union, a country with a record on human rights violations that is second to none. It is not inconceivable that five million innocent victims of the war in Afghanistan may some day be accused of war crimes and one can be sure that the Soviet Union will be more than willing to supply evidence against them.

VALUE ADDED TAX-CONSEQUENCES FOR SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Government is considering the possibility of introducing a value-added tax system to replace the federal sales tax. Such a decision would be disastrous for small businesses. The administrative costs would be very heavy, for exemptions would very likely create confusion. A value-added tax system would require 1.4 million new tax licenses and an extension of the bureaucracy.
One of the hundreds of promises which the Conservative Party had made before the September 4, 1984, election was to ease quickly and significantly the burden resulting from overwhelming regulations and red tape.
In Sherbrooke, on July 26, 1984, the Prime Minister stated: "Private sector is the engine of economic growth, and small and medium size businesses are its key elements". Now that he is in power, the same leader is entertaining the notion of setting up a tax system which would betray the promises he had made before the election.

subtopic: LIVESTOCK BLOOD-TYPING LABORATORY
LIVESTOCK BLOOD-TYPING LABORATORY
speechtext:
Mr, Speaker, last Thursday Agriculture Canada officials overruled the recommendations of the Department's study by announcing the privatization of the only cattle and horse blood-typing laboratory in Canada. This action shocked livestock breeders and could cost the industry millions of dollars.
Using the same principles of blood-typing used in human paternity suits, this lab solves disputes involving embryo transfers in cattle and resolves questions of parentage in expensive thoroughbred horses. Clearly, large amounts of money are at stake.
In view of this, and in view of the obvious need for the strict integrity, confidentiality, and continuity well provided by the federal lab, it seems absurd that this important service will be privatized on April 1. What makes it seem even more absurd is that the program did not cost the Government a cent. It was run on a break even basis.
Quite understandably, the breeders are worried and upset. They are concerned about the prospects of higher testing prices as a result of a private monopoly taking over, but they are also concerned about a sudden decline in international confidence in the records of Canadian breeders. On behalf of the cattle and horse breeders of Canada and on behalf of the livestock industry in general, I call for this decision to be rescinded immediately.

subtopic: COMMISSION'S DECISION TO SECURE EVIDENCE IN SOVIET UNION
COMMISSION'S DECISION TO SECURE EVIDENCE IN SOVIET UNION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Deschenes Commission decided that it would send representatives to the Soviet Union and Poland to obtain evidence on possible war criminals in Canada. In Edmonton,
80,000	Canadians of Ukrainian origin, as well as Canadians of Lithuanian, Latvian, Estonian and other origins are deeply concerned over this decision. This decision leaves me asking a number of questions about the safeguards and conditions requested by the Commission to protect our own citizens. Our primary concern should be to protect Canadians from potential falsified evidence used against them by the Soviet Union.
Can we trust Soviet authorities to respect the independence of our own inquiry? Will they not interfere with our Canadian legal traditions while the Commission is conducting examinations in the Soviet Union? If the Commission is to seek Soviet evidence then it must agree, first, to guarantee in writing that all documents are absolutely genuine; second, evidence heard by witnesses will be obtained according to Canadian law free
from Soviet interference; and, third, interpreters must be Canadian.
We should always be mindful that the Soviet Union has rewritten its own history to fit its own views and philosophy. The Commission should not use any information that cannot be verified through sources and evidence obtained in the democratic and free world. To do otherwise could condemn innocent Canadians.

subtopic: ST. CLAIR RIVER-TESTING OF WATER SAMPLES
ST. CLAIR RIVER-TESTING OF WATER SAMPLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to inform all Members and the Canadian public that the Ministry of the Environment tests of treated water samples at four St. Clair area water treatment plants have shown no detectable dioxins in any form. We are assured that the St. Clair River area drinking water poses no threat to our health.
I would like to applaud the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) for responding in a most responsible and effective manner. Mobilizing an urgent scientific investigation into the sources of chemicals and directing water samples to be taken every two hours are proof positive that the Government is committed to acting in a professional and positive manner on environmental concerns. The St. Clair River issue has been plagued by many who inaccurately reported the events. Such irresponsible actions have, unfortunately, caused undue stress for many and a possible blight on our community. This should never have happened. The Minister recognized this. He exercised great care to ensure that the reports were completely and professionally reported. The St. Clair River situation is being addressed by four Government agencies spending a total of $8 million over the next two years. Those who have spoken on this issue should make sure that they are bound by the standard practice of data quality assurance. Failure to do so indicates an unseemly haste to condemn an entire area by innuendo, a practice which serves no one.

subtopic: COMMISSION'S DECISION TO SECURE EVIDENCE IN SOVIET UNION
COMMISSION'S DECISION TO SECURE EVIDENCE IN SOVIET UNION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although Justice Jules Deschenes' decision on the taking of Soviet evidence has outlined several safeguards, it has ignored safeguards which must be in place before any agreement is reached.
Justice Deschenes makes no mention of the right of the accused to be represented by counsel and to receive notice. There is no mention that examination of evidence will be taken on neutral territory where forensic examination and verification of the authenticity of the documents will be guaranteed. There is no mention that witnesses should and would be free to travel to Canada to give their testimony, and that they and their families would be free from retribution after testifying.
Before any travel is undertaken all the conditions must be agreed to in writing, and all the conditions must be maintained. The slightest deviation from the conditions set out should immediately nullify the agreement. There can be no allowance for the taking of evidence by anyone other than Canadian authorities. Justice Deschenes' conclusion that, barring unforeseen circumstances, the evidence be elicited by deputy commissioners leaves the door wide open for Soviet authorities to impede the justice procedure.
The rights of Canadians must be protected, and every guarantee protecting those rights must be in writing. It is not enough to say that the Commission will insist that they be accepted and observed. All the conditions must be accepted in writing and observed, or they will not be worth the paper they are written on.

subtopic: PETROLEUM AND GAS REVENUE TAX ACT INCOME TAX ACT MEASURE TO AMEND

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mrs. McDougall that Bill C-82, an Act to amend the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act and the Income Tax Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: PETROLEUM AND GAS REVENUE TAX ACT INCOME TAX ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to join in the debate on Bill C-82 this afternoon because it provides us with an opportunity to appreciate important fiscal and economic matters which should be in the minds of the Canadian people. It provides us with an opportunity to appreciate the policy directions which the Government is taking. It gives us the opportunity to discover choices made by the Conservative Party, choices which will not redound, I suggest, to the prosperity of the country, choices which are very closely related to the fact that corporate enterprises in the country may do very well with the present Government. I suppose its leaders will be happy about that fact.

November 19, 1985
Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act
The ordinary people of Canada, the payers of taxes in the middle and lower ranges in particular, will suffer from the decisions which this Government has made. The result of the economic and social suffering they undergo will be to make Canada a poorer country than it might be. It will quite possibly have the effect of nipping in the bud this fragile recovery, some manifestations of which the Government is using so strongly to try to maintain its standing with the Canadian public.
We know that as far as the polls are concerned the Government is in some difficulty with the Canadian public and that its standing has fallen markedly. I suggest this afternoon, in the context of debating the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax, that that fall in public standing does not relate only to mistakes which Ministers made during September and October and evidences of Government bungling of matters as varied as the inspection of tuna in New Brunswick to the propping-up of a bank which should have been allowed to fall last March as a consequence of the mismanagement of that bank. I suggest that this fall in standing of the Government reflects choices which have been made, including the one that we are debating this afternoon, choices which will impoverish ordinary Canadians while enriching a small number of oil companies. These are companies which have done very well in the past and which will be pursuing the process of their own enrichment more and more strongly thanks to the decisions of the Government.
1 was interested to note before we rose for lunch the comments of the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) who commended friends and colleagues from my caucus for the fine tone the debate had taken between them. I hope this afternoon that in considering some of these questions we might maintain that particular level of debate, even if I do aim at the bone and marrow of Government policy in these matters in suggesting the nature and the consequences of decisions which the Government is taking.
If we are to appreciate the nature of Bill C-82, and if all Canadians who are watching us are to appreciate the nature of the Bill, it is necessary to look back over a dozen years or so of the petroleum industry in Canada and place this particular decision of the Government in context. It will be of no surprise to the Canadian people, nor to any of my colleagues here I would think, to suggest that what happened in the petroleum industry beginning about 1973 was one of the most incredible pieces of cartel action ever seen by the human population of this globe. The increase in petroleum prices which OPEC was able to carry through beginning in 1973-74 led to one of the most massive and certainly rapid transfers of wealth which we have ever seen. It had the effect of enriching producers of petroleum, initially perhaps the companies, but, in the Middle East in particular, also the owners of the resource, and a variety of countries and governments in the most remarkable way. Inevitably, given the global nature of the oil business, that impact was felt in Canada as well. Those who were experiencing this transfer, those who were paying the rise in costs of gasoline and other petroleum products, were faced with a situation in which wealth could end up in very few
hands or could very easily leave the country. In fact, during the 1970s that clearly happened. If one examines the figures for the petroleum industry, one will discover that the total revenues to be shared in 1975 were $5 billion. Two years later it had hit $7.5 billion. By 1979, it had reached $10.9 billion. These very rapid increases in revenue to the oil companies were taken from the petroleum users.
The question is, what should the Government do in these circumstances, are the oil companies to be enriched and able to transfer great amounts of capital out of Canada, or are the people of Canada to be able to share in this enormous economic rent, as the economists would surely label it? Whether or not it was possible for the people of Canada to share in the consequence of cartel action was a very important question which faced the Canadian Government in the late 1970s and early 1980s because the profits of the leading oil companies in Canada rose so very sharply. For example, the profits of Imperial Oil rose from $290 million in 1974 to $471 million in 1979, and they went as high as $601 million in 1980. That was a reflection of the consequences of the process I am describing.
During the 1970s the industry succeeded in holding percentages ranging from 56 per cent down to 45 per cent in 19771978 and down still more to 42 per cent in 1979, but then they rebounded in 1980 to 56 per cent of the revenues. The province took practically all of the rest. The federal Government received very little of this. It received 6 per cent of the total, a mere $300 million, in 1975. The percentage dropped to 4 per cent in 1977 and in 1980 it actually fell as low as minus 10 per cent. The Government ended up a net loser in the petroleum revenue sharing in which the people of Canada surely had a right to share. The oil companies made enormous gains which were largely transferred out of the country. The evidence from 1974 to 1980 is that there was a net capital export of $4.1 billion by the oil industry. It is in the context, then, of the oil companies largely involved in transferring these monopoly gains, the economic rent, out of the country. So the establishment of the petroleum and gas revenue tax in 1981 was a sensible decision by the Government. Its repeal now under Bill C-82 is a stupid decision, fiscally and economically, as one can appreciate in perusing these statistics. As a consequence of the changes carried through by our last Government it became possible for Ottawa to join in the sharing of these revenues which had resulted from the OPEC cartel power. In fact, in 1981 the federal Government was able to achieve a 22 per cent share of those revenues. In 1982 that went up to 26 per cent although the percentage and the absolute totals fell off from $5.3 billion in 1982 to $4.6 billion in 1983 and only $3.8 billion estimated for 1984.
The significant thing of this process of achieving some gain for the Government of Canada, for the people of Canada, out of the consequences of cartel success, was that the people of Canada were able to see the Government taking in revenues and using them for the great variety of national purposes for which the Government of Canada exists. The oil companies did not suffer from all of this. One of the quite remarkable
November 19, 1985

things is that the revenues of the petroleum industry continue to rise. In 1980 the revenues were $11.3 billion to be shared between industry, the provinces and Ottawa. In 1981 they increased by almost one-half, to $15.8 billion. In 1982 they shot up to $20.4 billion and then levelled off a little.
With respect to these incredible revenues coming to the industry for potential sharing, the significant thing is that in spite of the petroleum and gas revenue tax, the gains which the industry had after the tax was applied, continued to increase in absolute figures. In 1980 the industry had taken in $6.3 billion. The following year, under the tax, it took in $6.7 billion. In the following year the total rose to $9.4 billion and then to $10.6 billion and $11.6 billion. In fact, the industry was moving towards keeping one-half of the revenues which were produced from petroleum and gas in this country. That is evidence of the extent to which the industry continued to flourish in spite of the tax. During the years 1981 to 1983- that three-year period-the oil companies transferred out of this country another $3.5 billion.
The decision of the Conservative Government to cancel the petroleum and gas revenue tax means that this revenue will no longer come to Government to cover the costs of Government, that great variety of things we need to do, such as keeping family allowances indexed, maintaining the old age pension at the proper level, and covering the cost of Government mistakes like the $1 billion it is going to cost to take care of the depositors of the Canadian Commercial Bank. Perhaps even more things, such as job-creation activities, could be paid for by a fair sharing of this revenue.
It is the decision of the Conservative Government to allow the oil companies to take the boodle again, to operate on the same patterns of the early 1970s and the 1960s. It has decided to allow these companies and their shareholders to enrich themselves outside of the country while individual Canadians pay two cents per litre more for gasoline in September and an additional one cent per litre in January, the increase in the sales tax which the Liberals put through in October of 1984 and another percentage point on the sales tax in 1986, and so it is nickel and diming the Canadian people to death. It is loading more and more of the burden of taxation on individual Canadians while it lets the oil companies get away with these enormous amounts in profits. The oil companies are able to enjoy again the unrestricted use of the profits which result from cartel activity. Here is a Government which is prepared to sock it to individual Canadians, to take money out of their pockets, and restrict the amount of business which can be done in any community because of the levels of taxation which it imposes, while letting the oil companies-which are undoubtedly good supporters of the Conservatives at election time- run off with billions and billions of dollars, sweep it out of the country, making precious little contribution-as others have noted before me-to the economy of this country.
Those are the kinds of decisions the Conservatives have made. Do they care about ordinary Canadians? Don't make me laugh. Are they concerned about the profits of their corporate friends? Obviously. That is the point of the
Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act
petroleum and gas revenue tax changes which are before us this afternoon.
The Canadian people expected something different than that. The oil companies, I am sure did not. However, ordinary Canadians, the people who voted for the Conservatives on September of 1984, expected them to take a leading part in getting this country moving, not selling it out as the Government will do with this Bill. I speak in strongest opposition to this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I think I am entitled to make this comment. The Member who spoke talked about the revenues and the difficulty of giving $5.6 billion to the oil companies, as this Bill does, in the period until 1990. We must talk about where the federal Government is going to get the revenue. I would like to put on the record two letters which I have with respect to revenue sharing between the federal and provincial Governments. I wrote to Paul Tellier, then the Deputy Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, on June 27 of this year. My letter is very short. It reads:
Dear Mr. Tellier:
According to your Department's paper "Energy Policy Overview", it is estimated that the revenue sharing between the federal and provincial governments and industry for 1984 will be, in percentage terms, 17 per cent, 31 per cent and 52 per cent, respectively.

Thank you for your assistance in this matter.
This is very important, Mr. Speaker, because this is how the pie will be sliced up and this will be the way in which the federal Government can finance a lot of its social programs and so on. I received a reply on September 19 of this year from Mr. de Montigny Marchand who is the new Deputy Minister. It reads:
Dear Mr. Waddell:
Thank you for your letter of June 27, 1985, in which you requested information on energy revenue shares. You referred to EMR estimates for 1984 that were produced late last year, and asked how these figures compare to the shares under the Western Accord.
The Petroleum Monitoring Agency has recently published its annual monitoring survey for 1984. I understand you have received a copy of the report. It shows the following actual breakdown of revenues for 1984:
	$ Billion	%
Federal	3.4	14.9Provinces	7.3	31.5Industry	12.4	53.6
November 19, 1985
Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act
The differences between these results and the earlier departmental estimates to which you referred are the normal result of receiving more accurate data on which to base the calculations.
Although it is still too soon to know with any degree of certainty what the total revenues available for "sharing" or the percentage splits will be for 1985, we expect that the results will be quite similar to those for 1984.
With respect to projections beyond 1985-
This is after the Western Accord and after this Bill.
-we have produced several different, internal forecasts of energy revenues. However, in the midst of so much uncertainty regarding international oil prices, levels of domestic oil and gas production, export volumes and natural gas prices, these projections are highly speculative in nature and, in fact, could be very misleading. Therefore, no single forecast has been adopted as the "official" departmental forecast, and I am of the opinion that it would be inappropriate to put any on the public record at this time.
Yours sincerely, de Montigny Marchand
What he is telling me, and the point I raise, is that we are asked to approve $5.6 billion to be given to the oil companies without putting this tax on. We do not know what the federal Government's share will be. We do not know whether it will get less of a share or how much it will get. It is incredible that the Conservative Party, which was dedicated to freedom of information, will not release the information as to how much money the federal Government will get. Through this Bill we are, in fact, bankrupting the federal Treasury.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) a question with regard to the bank bail-outs that we keep hearing about. Mr. Speaker, 1 thank the Member for that question because it allows us to be quite clear about our position on this particular matter. I will say at the outset that the mistakes that were made last March are at the root of the difficulty. If there had been a thorough examination of the Canadian Commercial Bank, the kind of examination that could, I believe, have been undertaken over the weekend that the Government had, it would have been realized that the bank was beyond saving. Responsible Ministers of Finance who deserve the position that they have in the Canadian Government, recognizing that and appreciating that this amounted to 2.5 per cent of the assets of the Canadian banking system, which banking system has prided itself on its standard and probity in years past, would have said that the bank does not deserve to exist. They would have said that we should drive it into receivership. We should have had a royal
commission, or whatever you would choose in the way of an investigation, to determine how, in the history of Canadian banking, something of that sort could have happened. That commission could have been empowered to consider hardship cases among the depositors who were involved in the bank and could have been asked to recommend to the Government action that might have been taken in case of a genuine hardship.
Remember, Mr. Speaker, that we are dealing with depositors who have more than $60,000 in the bank because those with up to $60,000 on deposit are covered by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. If there were hardship cases among those who had more than $60,000 in the bank last March, let the Parliament of Canada consider what could be done. There is no question that we could have had a sound policy for dealing with the hardship cases and the Canadian people would not have had loaded upon them the consequence of mistakes made by Ministers of Finance and of stupid and naive decisions made last March which could lead those Ministers to resign their positions. The Canadian people would then not have to pay $1 billion for a bail-out in September resulting from the repeated assurances that the Canadian Commercial Bank was fine. Sometimes bad business is done, and when bad business is done Government does not prop it up and the people of Canada do not pay the shot.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to begin the final debate in this House on Bill C-49, an Act to amend the Criminal Code in relation to prostitution. I might say that this will be the first of three Bills which will reach the final stage of debate. In the ensuing days and weeks we will have a Bill before the House for final reading with respect to divorce, for amendment of the Judges Act, and very soon there will come into force and effect the new legislation which was passed in this House, Bill C-18, with respect to drunk driving.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the legislative committee which reviewed Bill C-49 made just one amendment to the Bill as introduced by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie). That amendment, which clarified the meaning of the application of the Bill to customers of prostitutes, was welcomed by the Government as a successful attempt to clarify a meaning which was somewhat nebulous.
The committee had the benefit of the evidence of witnesses both for and against the Bill. Their testimony has, for the most part, reinforced my belief that Bill C-49 is not only needed urgently, but that it is the only possible way to deal effectively and efficiently with the problems related to street soliciting for the purpose of prostitution. None of the witnesses heard by the committee seriously question that Bill C-49 is the only legal, constitutional and practical way to return to the residents of our major urban centres the freedom to enjoy their homes and the streets of their communities without the interference of those who now use those streets to buy and sell sex.
May I add at this point, Mr. Speaker, that I was very impressed by the fact that over the past few years included in the people who appeared before our committee were the mayors of every major city from Vancouver to Niagara Falls to Halifax to Toronto. These are duly elected officials who represent their constituents and with one exception-that is the mayor of the City of Ottawa-everyone agreed that this is a good Bill. May I also point out that Mayor Drapeau came from Montreal to appear before our committee to support this Bill in circumstances where the City of Montreal has a by-law.
There are some who are opposed to this Bill. Their numbers do not include the mayors of the major municipalities of Canada which are afflicted with the blight of street prostitution. With the one exception I mentioned, that of the outgoing mayor of Ottawa, the elected representatives of the people at the level of government most directly affected by the problem endorsed the Government's response. Moreover, the Minister of Justice has the support of the chief law officers of the Crown in the provinces, the Attorneys General, in his effort to deal with the problem. It is worth noting that the newly elected Attorney General of Ontario, the Hon. Ian Scott, wrote to express his support for this legislative initiative. It is unfortunate that his colleagues in this House do not choose to follow his advice.
The opposition to this Bill focuses essentially on two criticisms; first, that the Bill does not deal with all of the problems associated with prostitution, including those relating to the exploitation of children and to the economic status of prostitutes. The second criticism is that the Bill creates a risk of abuse by the police. I would like once again to respond to these concerns. First, it is not, and it has never been, the objective of Bill C-49 to deal with all aspects of prostitution. What we are going to do is review the Badgley Report, and the report of the Fraser Committee, and in the new year there will be more legislation with respect to this particular topic. The purpose of this Bill is, plainly and simply, to deal with the very serious situation which exists in many cities in Canada, that of street solicitation.
Despite the evidence, a few persons continue to maintain that this is a minor problem. With respect, I cannot agree. Both in the view of the Fraser Committee and in the view of the citizens who are living with the problem on a day-to-day basis, it has been proven beyond any doubt that other legal and non-legal administrative means cannot deal effectively with the situation. That is not to say that social and economic approaches should not be undertaken to deal with the problems associated with prostitution but, first and foremost, we need a strong and forceful law to deal with the urgent problem of public prostitution which faces communities across Canada. Proposals for response to other problems associated with prostitution are under review. These other recommendations, as I said, will be coming forward in the new year.
With respect to the argument that Bill C-49 hypothetically could be abused by the police, there is always an element of risk when criminal law is used for the protection of the public interest. This is true for the enforcement of any sanction involving the Criminal Code.
Nothing in this Bill alters the fundamental rights of Canadians guaranteed by the Charter. Nothing in the Bill changes the basic substantive, procedural and evidentiary rights enjoyed by anyone suspected of an offence in the country. A lawful arrest requires reasonable and probable grounds to believe that an offence has been committed and the prosecution must prove every element of the offence beyond a reasonable doubt. The courts have made it clear that the control of soliciting for the purpose of prostitution is a function of the criminal law. The provinces and the municipalities do not have
November 19, 1985

the legislative authority to resolve the problem. That responsibility rests with Parliament and we have an obligation to the public to exercise our duty.
May 1 very briefly, Mr. Speaker, tell the House a little about the history of the Criminal Code as it affects prostitution and street soliciting. During the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries there evolved in England, for reasons I am not sure I can tell you about, a notion of what was called a "street walker". When our Criminal Code was codified in 1892 it contained certain offences known as vagrancy offences. No matter how the Criminal Code changed in terms of numbers, there was always the section with respect to vagrancy.
This law was in effect until 1972 and, although it was a very, very effective law, many of us felt that it was not a good law because it said that anyone who was known as a common prostitute and who loitered in a public place had to give the police a good account of herself or else she would be convicted of an offence. In many cases in those days prostitutes were picked up on the street, there were disputes as to the accounts they gave of themselves and it became, quite literally, a status offence. It was decided in 1972 that, as effective as this law was, it was not a good law. We changed the law in Parliament in that year and as a result of a judicial decision made in 1978 on what the word "soliciting" meant, it was decided that the conduct had to be "pressing and persistent". To this day, in spite of many, many cases that have gone to the Supreme Court of Canada, people still do not know precisely what the limit of "pressing and persistent" is.
As a result the Fraser report said that there is no doubt that there has to be a change in the law. It is not something that should be dealt with by way of municipal by-laws but is the responsibility of Parliament. There is no doubt, as evidenced by the surveys which were taken by the Fraser Commission, that 84 per cent of the people wanted something to happen in order that we could enforce a law with respect to prostitutes in the streets of our major cities because they are an absolute blight. Whether the political persuasion of people was NDP, such as that of the Mayor of Vancouver, or Conservative, or Liberal as it is in the City of Toronto, all of the duly elected mayors came before committees and said that we must do something.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that this law which we are about to implement is going to be an effective law. It is an important law. Let us not lose sight of the fact that it is not the be-all and end-all. It is not an express train to Utopia. It is meant to be an effective law to clean up the streets of our major cities so that people can enjoy freedom from interference.
I am very happy that after two weeks in committee and a debate on second reading we have reached the final stages without amendment. I hope that there is expenditious passage of this Bill. I hope that Members of the House agree with me in order that we can get it through as quickly as possible and ensure that it is in full force and effect very, very soon.

speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of reviewing the role of the Farm Credit Corporation, in order to make clear to the farming community, its position vis-a-vis other lending institutions.
He said: Mr. Speaker, thank you for this opportunity to introduce my motion in the House. Last April 23 I asked that the role of Canada's Farm Credit Corporation be re-examined so as to shed light on its position concerning farmers and Canadian financial institutions. I think that, in the not too distant future, we will have to define more clearly what this Crown corporation can do to help the many Canadian farmers who are in dire financial straits. As spokesman for a riding where most residents earn their living on farms, I think it is imperative to take action.
Mr. Speaker, the first thing to do is to explain the situation the farming community was in when the Progressive Conservative Party took office, and the best way to do that is to ask Hon. Members a few questions.
Among other things, for instance, do you know that between 1961 and 1981 the price of land rose four times faster than the price of farm products? Do you think it is easy to turn a farm business into a paying proposition under such circumstances? Do you also know that, according to a 1984 Farm Credit Corporation survey, close to 20 per cent of Canadian farmers experience serious financial problems? Do you also know that farm investments controlled by Canadian farmers declined by $1.2 billion-that is 1 per cent between 1981 and 1984- whereas the consumer price index jumped from 100 in 1981 to 124 in 1984?
Perhaps Hon. Members are wondering why I should be so concerned over these figures? Maybe I should sit down and let my western Canada colleagues have the floor, because they have been pushing the panic button all these years? Well, no way! In my own riding, in my own area, farmers are faced with serious problems, and an organization such as the Farm Credit Corporation could provide them with a more structured and efficient assistance.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a few more questions: Have you ever heard about the Movement for the Survival of Farmers? Have you ever heard about la Cour des miracles'? I am not joking; this is serious indeed! Such a thing exists in my own riding. It is an organization of Quebec farmers faced with financial difficulties. Have you ever heard of Mr. Marcel Talbot? Well, in August 1984, during the election campaign,
November 19, 1985

this man and a number of others, including Jean-Claude Boucher, went on a hunger strike in Saint-Cyrille de Wendov-er, in the Drummond riding. This man and the other strikers who were involved in various farming ventures had a great many horror stories to tell about their financial predicaments.
Mr. Speaker, I have also a number of press clippings-you can see that I have several of them-which I have collected in my area and especially from Mr. Gerald Prince, a journalist with the La Tribune newspaper. 1 used these clippings as a basis for my remarks.
To understand the important role which the Farm Credit Corporation could play today, we should look at the important role it played in earlier times. For instance, when its ancestor the Canadian Farm Loan Board was established in 1927, it was for very specific reasons. Canadian farmers were facing a very difficult situation. They were compelled to take short term loans at very high interest rates. Do you think the situation today is quite different? In order to address this problem, the Government established the Canadian Farm Loan Board. For 32 years, farmers could rely on an institution which adequately met their needs.
During this period, agriculture also experienced unprecedented growth. During the 50's, the whole context of agricultural financing changed. The situation became very different. The Canadian Farm Loan Board was granting loans nearly exclusively to consolidate middle term debts into long term debts. There were no lenders to serve newcomers in agriculture and farmers wishing to expand or modernize their farm. Have things really changed? The Board was no longer playing the dynamic role for which it had been created. Its terms of reference had to be changed and this is what the Government of Mr. Diefenbaker did in 1959. Desperate ills demand desperate measures. A new Act was passed and the Farm Credit Corporation was created. To give it the tools it required to be effective, the Conservative Government of the time increased the maximum amount of loans. It allowed the FCC to grant loans to farmers with lower net assets if they were willing to have their management methods monitored.
In 1964, the Farm Credit Act was amended to allow the FCC to lend money to associations of farmers and promote the pooling of financial resources. In the same spirit, the Act was again amended in 1975 to make it easier for new farmers to get started. This amendment allowed them to continue to have outside income in addition to their farming income during the first five years of the term of the loan.
By creating the Farm Credit Corporation, the Government put in place all the elements required to achieve the growth we have seen in Canadian agriculture since the beginning of the 60's until approximately three years ago.
It is interesting to note that, very soon after its creation, the Farm Credit Corporation held a large share of the farm credit market. As soon as 1965, it held 69 per cent of the market. I
Farm Credit Corporation
would like to point out that its share has now gone down to less than 25 per cent.
The 70's were certainly prosperous times. The value of land increased constantly and interest rates remained relatively low. In absolute figures, people often borrowed large amounts instead of using their capital because it was more economical to do so.
The arrival of the banks on the farm credit market was beneficial. They were able to offer middle and short term loans. Many farmers, after acquiring healthy net assets, no longer needed the security offered by long term loans.
They therefore turned to the banks because, even though their long term interest rates were higher than those of the corporation, their short and middle term rates were very attractive. This led many farmers to do business with them. This proved to be by far the most advantageous method of financing until interest rates began to climb. From then on, many farmers started to feel the pinch and have a lot of difficulty balancing their budget.
Moreover, at the same time the sales of farm products began to slow down and the growth of the 70's was replaced by a slow compression of incomes. Exports went down significantly, the production capacity of producers began increasing and prices fell.
The Farm Credit Corporation no longer plays the role which farmers expect it to play. It has been overtaken by the changes which have occurred in the financial structure of Canadian farming.
It is not recently that the situation of farmers has begun to deteriorate. The Government should have taken action three years ago, but it did nothing.
In 1959, when the corporation was created, there was a major problem which it helped to solve. Sources of financing and funds available for farm credit were inadequate. Today, we know that there is no shortage of money for lending.
Farmers are now facing another problem. Their level of indebtedness is too high. In addition, their incomes are not high enough to enable them to repay their debts. The problem also is that capitalization costs are too high and young farmers have to mortgage all their assets.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what happens to a pork producer when the selling price falls? What will happen to an apple producer in my riding when he incurs a $100,000 loss as a result of an early spring frost in April as it happened in 1981? Yes, a compensation was paid but three years later. Fortunately for that apple producer, Mr. Omer Blanchard, he had over 30 years of experience. What would have happened if a young man had bought that business one, two or five years ago?

Farm Credit Corporation
Do you know also that 60 per cent of farm bankruptcies in Quebec in 1983-84 occurred within 40 miles from Drummond-ville? And according to the newspaper La terre de chez-nous which reported those statistics, they were generally well-equipped farms with new crops and producers arriving late on that market. Now where are the lenders who could have helped those farmers during those gloomy days? Do you not think that should be the actual role to be played by the Farm Credit Corporation?
The Farm Credit Corporation should be in a position to face the true problems and find original and effective solutions. It should not go on granting loans along the same old lines. The assets of a farmer should be better managed to increase his net worth as quickly as possible. Thus, a farmer would be in a stronger position.
It is known that one of the major problems faced by farmers since the beginning of times is income fluctuation. Their incomes fluctuate with the weather, with production elsewhere in the world, and with the prices they get. In economic terms, that is reflected in cash flow problems. It is imperative that the Farm Credit Corporation develop ways of repayment that would allow farmers to compromise with those kinds of situations.
Formerly, the solution was to arrange a loan at the lowest possible rate, with the longest possible term, in order to stabilize the expenses. The corporation is offering a product based on that model, which has already proved to be efficient but is now obsolete, because the terms and conditions of the loans it is offering do not meet with the particular needs of farmers anymore. In order to become efficient, the corporation would have to be provided with the means to reduce its interest rates to make them compatible with actual farm income, the actual income derived by a farmer from his investment.
In a column written by Mr. Andre Goulet in the Drum-mondville newspaper L'Express of November 12, 1985- which is very recent, only last week-reference is made to the case of Mario Sarrazin, a 21-year-old from Wickham, a very beautiful community in my constituency. From a very early age, he has been helping his father on the family farm, a beautiful farm with a hundred or so heads of Holstein cattle. In Quebec, the dairy cows that belong to the Sarrazin families-and I say families because there is more than one on the same range in Wickham, and they are tremendously successful-the Sarrazin dairy cows have an excellent reputation, and the prizes they have won over the years point to that high quality. Also, young Mario often meets with foreign visitors, even from Europe, who come to benefit from his father's expertise.
So you may ask me what is so special about Mario Sarrazin? You may not think there is anything really special, except that he is taking over from his father. At least he would like to, after finishing high school. 1 believe he studied farming techniques at the CEGEP de Victoriaville, and went through
farm administration and management training sessions. He has also been through a practical training period on another farm, in order to further his practical experience. He will also be attending this week, on November 22, 23, and 24, a provincial seminar on "The place of young people in farming".
So what did young Mario, age 21, have to say to the reporters? He referred, like any other farmer, to the high cost of investment, high risk income, loans and variable interest rates, the scarcity of farm labour, the high cost of quotas, which in many cases exceed the value of the farm itself. So this is what Mario had to say in connection with his own plans. Is that not what is on the mind of a very serious young businessman?
1 would like to ask the Hon. Member for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Tardif) who in this House would dare to launch a business costing $500,000, $700,000 or even a million dollars if he risks losing everything after a few years because of a natural disaster or the fluctuation of the interest rates? Who in this House would be willing to say: "1 can lend Mario the money he needs?1
What do these young people like Mario need? They need the lowest possible interest rates because they must invest very large amounts at first. They need help in managing the financial aspects of their business. If we could help them to get through the first five years without too many problems, 1 am convinced that the future would not be as bleak as it now seems for our young farmers.
There is work to do because the Farm Credit Corporation could be a lot more effective than it is now. However, it needs a lot of flexibility. Its programs are outdated and are no longer adequate to meet the needs of farmers.
Mr. Speaker, all realistic and intelligent solutions will receive my support. 1 believe that it is possible to make a positive contribution to change this situation without spending enormous amounts of money. However, we must act; otherwise, if it remains unchanged for years, what encouragement can I give the potato producers of my constituency? What can I tell the thousands of dairy producers who deliver their milk to Agropur? What can 1 tell the pork producers of my region, whose largest slaughterhouse is called Olympia and has annual sales of $300 million?
We have to take action so that the Farm Credit Corporation will stop having about $600 million to lend with no takers. This is ridiculous. We must not forget that only 5 per cent of Canadians produce the food needed to feed the remaining 95 per cent of the population. If we don't back them up, our supplies in food products will be at stake.
