Mr. Speaker, 1 am very pleased to have an opportunity to speak to this motion. First of all, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Drummond (Mr. Guilbault) on his motion, and I realize how relevant his words are, since the Hon. Member's riding is next to mine, and 1 know that in both ridings, agriculture is one of the major industries, and that the situation of many Quebec farmers is simply appalling.
Mr. Speaker, I get the impression, after listening very carefully to the Hon. Member's speech, that he is acting on, and as a result of, pressure from and meetings with producers and farmers, and informing Hon. Members of the nature of the problems they are facing. Unfortunately, it seems to me the action he is taking is not quite strong enough and his objectives are scarcely defined and even rather obscure, if we consider how the Hon. Member is presenting the issue. For the sake of argument, I shall, if I may, read the motion before the House.
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of reviewing the role of the Farm Credit Corporation, in order to make clear to the farming community, its position vis-a-vis other lending institutions.
You will agree that upon reading the motion, I had to wonder about the significance and the meaning of the motion, and also after listening to the Hon. Member for Drummond who, I admit, gave a pretty accurate and a pretty honest description of the kind of problems farmers are facing. Considering these extremely critical and extremely urgent concerns, I deplore the fact that we do not have a motion before the House today that defines objectives and suggests some concrete ways of dealing with the problems the Hon. Member's constituents and mine are facing, problems that exist in the vast majority of Quebec ridings and everywhere else in this country.
Mr. Speaker, the fact is that during the election campaign, formal and concrete commitments were made which recognized the need to redefine the mandate of the Farm Credit Corporation. Everyone agreed at the time that since the situation and changed, the Corporation as such no longer played the role it was supposed to play in meeting the farmers' needs. The Government knows the problems, it knows where the difficulties lie, and in fact it is aware of a number of solutions that could be suggested. Now, after a year and some months in power, they are presenting a motion that seems to be very obscure and fails to propose anything that is the least bit concrete or significant. The only attempt to deal with this problem since the new Government came to power consisted in reducing the interest rate by a few percentage points. I remember statements by people in the industry in which they said it was very restrictive, very selective, and that in the final instance, these were just a few trifles, and that Quebec farmers could do without these trifles. What they needed was concrete solutions to their problems.
Farm Credit Corporation
1 think that the motion as such is very relevant and deserves support for its objectives and its potential for bringing about, 1 hope, some improvement, however minor, in the present situation. However, I think that when the Farm Credit Corporation is being discussed we have in the first place to accept or acknowledge a number of premises which seem to me to be absolutely essential and basic, premises which should acknowledge that farming or the food producing sector is a basis priority in our society.
We must also admit that our society cannot get along without the farming community, a sector which must have the priority and face a series of problems and barriers against which we absolutely cannot do anything. I refer of course to the weather, the international markets, a set of barriers which our farmers must face but which remain beyond their control. Now as a result of that reality or that premise, I think that we should consider the future while keeping those absolutely essential facts in mind.
The present situation is simply disastrous. I remember that a few months before it was defeated, the former government had introduced in the House a Bill to improve considerably the lot of farmers, those especially who had obligations they simply could not meet. 1 have always been quite surprised to see this corporation which administers public funds for the purpose not of helping agriculture but seemingly of killing it. 1 could give a whole series of examples.
Fairly recently, 1 asked the Chairman of the Committee on Agriculture how much it cost annually the Department, the Corporation, to repossess farms. In other words, my question was this: When the Corporation repossesses a farm which it was financing, does it recover its costs? When it sells the farm at a later date, does it recover its investments? The Chairman did not hesitate: No, the Corporation loses tens of millions of dollars every year because when it repossesses a farm, such a farm is abandoned for a period of one, two, three, four years and, when it is finally resold, the sale price is considerably lower than the amount guaranteed. Under such circumstances ... statistical data are there to prove it... the Corporation is worse than the banks. Why is not the Corporation doing what the banks are doing?
When the going gets tough, when a real problem occurs, a person goes to his or her banker, explains the situation and submits a proposal for settlement, a plan for the next few years. Often, not to say most of the time, the banker will make concession, increase grant delays to help the debtor reimburse his debt, and even reduce the principal owed to the financial institution. This will sometime give the person breathing space, as well as the desire to continue and save his business. So when a farmer is faced with similar difficulties, there is absolutely nothing he can hope for from the Corporation in terms of compromise, because all he hears is this: You owe us money, you pay; failing which, we will seize your property.

November 19, 1985
Farm Credit Corporation
Currently, I am dealing with a number of cases one of which seems to me absolutely unbelievable. It involves a small farm that this gentleman is operating with his wife and children, the value of which clearly exceeds $100,000. That farmer has no other debt than his loan from the Farm Credit Corporation, which comes close to $50,000. That man had an accident while cutting his wood for the winter, so he was forced to let go his operations over a period of some months. He fell behind and failed to meet his instalment. He went to the Farm Credit Corporation, and all these people could find to say to that man was: "Sell part of your farm or part of your quota and you will have the money for your instalment".
How ridiculous, how grossly unacceptable can that be! There is no sympathy whatsoever for an undertaking which from the start is viable, which has no financial difficulty of any sort, where the operator has just suffered an accident, and which could perfectly well have regained its viability without any problem whatsoever. But nonetheless, that man was asked to forsake a part of his income, a part of his quota, or to sell a part of his land.
This is simply ridiculous. No banker would have dared propose such a thing that verges on indecency.
I am amazed, now that 15 months have already gone by, that this Government has not taken concrete steps to introduce a specific piece of legislation with really identifiable goals, that would give the Farm Credit Corporation a new mandate because the corporation could make a really worthwhile, relevant contribution to the maintenance and development of our agro-food industry.
I am also concerned, since no such legislation has been introduced to this day, about a few statements made by the Minister to the effect that free trade was the new challenge for Canada. What concerns me is that the dairy policy that was to be announced on August 1st is not yet known on this 19th day of November. 1 am concerned because a firm commitment was made to pay a substantial amount to hog producers. It has not been done yet. Besides, they gave up on that one a long time ago.
I am concerned because the Minister seems to consider the agricultural sector in the same way as all other economic sectors, like the small and medium-sized businesses, like the manufacturing of chairs and desks, or furniture, in fact like all other sectors of economic activity.
Once you have reached the stage where you consider the future in that light, there is reason for concern and it is even tragic for those who have huge financial obligations to meet within the next months or years.
I say to myself that in our statements and in our political customs, we agree to help private enterprise through grants. We agree to encourage a company to establish itself in a
specific area by contributing up to 50 per cent, 60 per cent or 70 per cent, in some cases, of the business or entrepreneur's investment. And the amount that is provided or given to the company is a payment in cash made within the year following the setting up of the business or industry. The yield on that investment that is called grant is translated of course in job creation and spin-offs generated by those new jobs. To this I agree wholeheartedly. As a policy, it appears essential to me, a vital contribution to regional development.
However, from the moment we accept this approach towards supporting private industry, it seems to me that we should be even more generous, more interested by the agrifood industry since society needs and will always need farmers, and the consumer will always need a healthy, lively and very dynamic agricultural sector.
We accept to make enormous concessions to oil multinational companies apparently, and rightly, to generate employment. Yet we are very hesitant and really neglectful about giving farmers what they fully deserve, what they absolutely need.
In my opinion, as I said before, we should redefine in depth the role of the Farm Credit Corporation. We should give it a completely different direction where its fundamental purpose would be to support and to help directly and indirectly by the agri-food industry under all its forms. The present reality is however completely different.
That direction, that redefining of the corporation should be based first on a reduced interest rate, which should not exceed a real rate of 5 per cent, in my opinion. That is to say 5 per cent plus inflation, up a maximum of 8 per cent. For example, should the inflation rate be 2 per cent one year, the interest rate on loans would be 7 per cent.
In this way, it would not be very costly and furthermore, in my opinion, it would be less than what we are presently giving to the small and medium-sized businesses and to industry as a whole.
The advantage or the consequence of such a redefinition would be an agri-food industry in which people would invest. In agriculture investment also means new jobs, increased exports, better productivity and a whole range of positive improvements in the economy. It seems to me very important that we recognize the very particular nature of farming.
We are willing to help the business sector, but when it comes to the agri-food industry we are far less generous and more reluctant to provide the help which, obviously, is so badly needed.
I regret to say that farmers are presently in a situation where the future is more like the great unknown. It looks very worrisome. And you know, as well as I do, that people who are traumatized, who are worried, who do not know what future holds for them do not invest and are far less determined in the way they work and produce.

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, personally, I want to support the motion so that it can go through, as I hope, as quickly as possible. 1 also wish that in the next few days, weeks and months, we will be able to improve it so that there will be practical solutions to the very real problems that were outlined by the Hon. Member for Drummond (Mr. Guilbault), and there will soon be applied remedial action to bring back confidence in that sector that society cannot do without.
At the present time, the Farm Credit Corporation is considered in Quebec somewhat as a Shylock. Nobody wants to have anything to do with it, except as a last resort.
Indeed, as confirmed by statistics, the Farm Credit Corporation is not very much present in Quebec, not to say totally absent. I think that if we redefined the role of the Corporation, it could become an instrument for development and promotion, for the greatest benefit of Quebec's as well as Canada's agriculture, and for the greatest benefit of society which obviously includes all electors and consumers.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FARM CREDIT CORPORATION ROLE OF THE CORPORATION VIS-A-VIS OTHER LENDING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Drummond (Mr. Guilbault) for bringing this motion before the House. It is something that we can support. I suppose it is a motherhoodlike motion in that it asks the Government to consider the advisability of reviewing the role of the Farm Credit Corporation in order to make clear to the farming community its possible position relative to other lending institutions.
Because the Farm Credit Corporation has not fulfilled its mandate for providing adequate financing to a very depressed farm industry in the last few years, there is no doubt that we need to look at the issue again. Consequently, I believe it is very important that this motion at least be passed so that it may give some direction to the Government.
In the process of discussing this motion, it would become us to bring forward some of the situations in agriculture that are causing the kinds of problems we are seeing. I suggest that the debt that farmers carry, something around $22 billion these days, is a symptom of the problem and not really the problem itself. If we had an agricultural structure with some stability and security, the farmers would not have that kind of debt. The amount of farm debt can be found in every statistic at which one can look regarding agriculture.
The Farm Credit Corporation issued a press release some time ago which suggested there should be a real concern in the agricultural industry in recognizing that the high-debt low-equity group of farmers comprise the most productive group of farmers in Canada and that one-third of the farmers who have the lowest equity are responsible for the largest share of farm sales. On the surface of it, that is not surprising because the statistic indicates that a large group of those farmers are probably the young farmers who are just getting started and consequently may be more aggressive about the way in which they farm. At the same time, we must recognize that many of
Farm Credit Corporation
those farmers are being forced to produce more than they really think they should from the same land and in that process are mining the soil rather than building it up.
The presentation to which I just referred also indicated that except for Quebec farmers, low-equity farmers borrow more than they invest in their capital purchases. In other words, statistically most farmers who are borrowing the most or have very little equity and high debts borrow money to operate. That is the thing about which we should be worrying.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture made a presentation not too many weeks ago in which it made the same suggestion as the one contained in this motion. The Federation suggested that we need to review the role of the Farm Credit Corporation as a lending institution for farmers. It was indicated that the idea of the Farm Credit Corporation being a body of last resort is not what the Farm Credit Corporation was mandated to be and therefore we should be looking at what happened to it and what we can do to return the Farm Credit Corporation to a position in which it will be the source of funds that are needed for farming. Therefore, I agree with and support this motion and suggest that the Government get with it and move in that particular direction.
Doing something about the Farm Credit Corporation so that it can make more money available to finance the farming community will not solve the problem in agriculture. Debt is a symptom of the real problem and is not the problem itself.
We should realize that there must have been a time when the farming community was doing well. There have been a few years in the last 20 years when the farming community has done well. In 1973, for example, everyone thought the farming community was on its way up and that there was no way to stop it. The statistics for the years 1943 to 1953 show that farmers received an average of about 6.6 per cent of the national income. Those were the 10 years immediately after the war. At that time, there was a certain amount of stability and growth in the farming community. It is very interesting to note that during that time, most people in this country felt that there was a balanced economy because no group was doing particularly better than any other group. Farmers were doing pretty well, small businessmen were doing pretty well and even those earning rental income were doing pretty well. The corporations that had had some difficulties during the War were re-establishing themselves and were doing pretty well. The banks did not complain. They were not doing as well as they are doing now but they did not complain. The employees of all of these groups, unionized and non-unionized, felt that they were getting a fair share of the national income.
Let us look at what happened in the next 20 or 30 years. Between 1943 and 1952, the economy seemed to be very stable and the average portion of the national income earned by farmers was, as I mentioned, 6.6 per cent. Since that time, the portion of national income going to farmers has been declining. In 1983, the farmer's portion of the national income was .5 per cent. It went up in 1984, I understand, to 1 per cent. Perhaps the portion of everyone's income fell as dramatically as well, but obviously it did not because someone has to use up

November 19, 1985
Farm Credit Corporation
that 100 per cent of income. By the way, that is a reduction for the farmers of 84.9 per cent. We wonder why they are in trouble and why they are borrowing money.
Let us look at the other side of this matter. Back in 1943, the banks collected 1.26 per cent of the national income in interest payments. By 1983-84, they were collecting 9.7 per cent of the national income. In other words, while the farmer's portion of the income went down by 85 per cent, the financial institutions' portion went up by 662 per cent. So their portion of the national income was increased by 660 per cent while the portion of farmers went down to 85 per cent. Surprisingly, when compared to financial institutions other groups which have been in trouble are not doing as well. I will deal with this now although it is not the topic today. It is rather worth-while to consider. For instance, in the period 1943-1953 small business took in 10.5 per cent of the national income. In 1983-84 small business was down to 4.3 per cent of the national income. In other words, small business has decreased its share of the national income by 59 per cent. This is not as large a reduction as that seen in the agricultural industry but it is a significant one.
One group which has stayed fairly level is that group which deals with compensation to employees. During and after the war years the salaries of people employed in union and nonunion jobs was 66 per cent of the national income. Some 30 years later they now take in 73 per cent of the national income. They have increased their take by 10.9 per cent.
In terms of agriculture, we need not consider the displacement of the national banking operation in order to turn that debt over to the Farm Credit Corporation. We must not ignore the system in which we live because we have to work within that system. However, let us do something more concrete in terms of the agricultural industry. Let us not continue with reductions in this sector, although I do not know how it can be reduced much more when it is already down to 1 per cent of the national income. I do not know how one can go much lower and still survive, which is the problem with which we are faced. I am sure the Hon. Member for Drummond brought forward his motion on the basis which I am now pointing out. We must do something now about the agricultural industry. We must do something about that one-third of young farmers who have the lowest equity and the highest debt and who produce a good portion of our products. If we do not do something about this problem then these farmers will be lost to the agricultural industry. If this review of the Farm Credit Corporation will start us in the right direction toward some type of comprehensive solution to the farming problem along with stabilization, parity pricing and other issues, then we should carry it out. We should not leave the industry in the state it is in presently.
It is interesting to note that farmers have only two possibilities. They can either increase the price of their products or they can decrease their input. Over the last few years in the farming community interest on debt has increased by 322 per
cent. The cost of petroleum products has increased by 284 per cent while the cost of fertilizer has increased by 218 per cent. The cost of chemicals has increased by 274 per cent. If one were to take the time to add up those figures it would be seen that for over 30 years total operating expenses for farming have increased by 1,053 per cent. During the same period of time the total receipts have only increased by some 688 per cent. This leaves a deficit of 365 per cent, which illustrates the point I have been making all along. We used to receive 6 per cent of the national income and now we receive only 1 per cent. The 365 per cent deficit with respect to reduction, in terms of actual intake compared with what we used to make per dollar spent and what we now make, has just about disappeared. I hesitate to say that by the year 1985 we will be down to 0 per cent as far as our portion of the national income is concerned. That is to say, we will be spending as much on debt as we will be taking in. That will be the case even when we take in dairy farmers, who are at least getting by.
Although I support the motion which is before us, I would have supported it more enthusiastically had it contained a resolution suggesting that the Government take a look at the pricing structure in terms of the whole agricultural industry. Regardless of whether this review is done in part or in whole it will result in us looking at every part of the agricultural industry if we expect it to survive in the way in which we think it should survive.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-U.S.S.R.-EMIGRATION OF JEWS
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-U.S.S.R.-EMIGRATION OF JEWS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 28 last I asked the Parliamentary Secretary, in the
November 19, 1985

absence of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), about word which was coming out of Israel that Russia might be relenting and letting some of the Soviet Jews emigrate to Israel, Canada and other countries. We were encouraged by that piece of news. I asked the Parliamentary Secretary whether there was any foundation for our very strong hope that this might be true. Regrettably, it does not appear that there is any foundation to it. However, I look forward to the Parliamentary Secretary's response in which he may have something further to add.
Tragically, the number of Jews being permitted to leave Russia has dropped to a mere trickle in the last few months and years. I hope that if there is some foundation to the rumour, if I may call it that, it is simply not a public relations attempt on the eve of the Geneva conference. This is really a human rights issue. Russia, of course, was a signatory of the 1975 Helsinki Accord. We are pressing the Soviets to honour their word and allow refusniks to leave the country. I would like to make a number of remarks on this issue.
From time to time we have heard bits of good news in this regard. I heard recently that Yelena Bonner, wife of Nobel Peace Prize Laureate Andrei Sakharov, will be released from exile in the Soviet Union and will be allowed to go to the West for medical treatment. That is good news. There is also news which is not so good. It concerns people such as Andrei Sakharov and Anatoly Shcharansky, who is only 37 years of age. These men have been jailed or subjected to internal exile for years. They are both sick and the indications are they have been subjected to mindbending drug torture. Their terrible crimes include daring to ask the Soviet Government to honour its Constitution on citizens' rights in the 1975 Helsinki Accord on Human Rights.
There are many organizations and many individuals who work very hard on behalf of the Soviet Jews. There is an organization in Ottawa called the Canadian Parliamentary Group for Soviet Jewry. It has, I believe, some 272 members from both the House of Commons and the other place. We are honoured to have a person like the Hon. Member for Edmonton Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour) as Chairman of that group. I am honoured to be one of the seven-person executive committee.
Different steps have been taken over the last year. There was a special trip to Russia to plead the case of Soviet Jews. Our Chairman, the Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona, sent a letter to President Reagan on the eve of the Geneva Conference and I would like to quote the last paragraph of that letter:
We wish to assure you of the support which exists in Canada for Soviet Jews. We trust that on this issue you will speak with Mikhail Gorbachev on behalf of all peoples concerned with human rights.
The National Council of Jewish Women of Canada is also very active. It has a separate committee on world Jewry headed by Eti Young. In Don Valley East there are several residents who are very concerned and hard working on this issue. I think of people like Mrs. Patti Starr, Mrs. Arlene
Adjournment Debate
Goldwater and Mrs. Joyce Zweig. It was Arlene Goldwater who introduced me to my refusnik. I have adopted a refusnik. His name is Simon Shnirman. He was born in 1957. He married his wife Leah in 1983 and they have a daughter Yona whom Simon has not yet seen.
One of Simon's recent crimes is that he gave two postcards, probably blank, which he had received through the mail, to one of the prisoners, and he washed his clothes by hand after working hours at a time and place not intended for this purpose. For these crimes he was given five days in an isolation cell without food or drink. For the past two years in the labour camp he has suffered great harassment and has been asked to do the hardest jobs. His basic right to receive packages has been denied. I could go on with the various forms of harassment but time is not available.
I wrote to his wife Leah on April 17, 1985 to basically introduce myself and give her a bit of my background. I mentioned the four children my wife Sandy and I have and the grandchild we were expecting. I was thrilled on August 21 to receive a letter, via Joyce Zweig, from Leah. Time does not permit me to read everything in the letter but I would like to quote just one part as follows:
God knows I tell the truth. Simon is not well, I am afraid of his health. He needs now, and after this camp of strict regime, good medical help. I thank you for your supporting and hope you won't forget us in this difficult time.
This is an important issue, Mr. Speaker; it is a human rights issue.
I recently had a letter from Eti Young concerning a telegram that had been sent to three officials in Russia on Simon Shnirman's behalf. The National Council of Jewish Women, the Soviet Jewry Committee, has adopted Simon as its refusnik in the Toronto area. The Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour) and I jointly signed a letter to the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) which was sent on September 25, 1985 pleading the case of Simon. This is just one individual, Mr. Speaker, but an important one.
There is a family network in Canada working on behalf of these important people. We ask the people of Canada to lend their prayerful support to the plight of these people in Russia whose only crime, in most cases, is simply wanting to speak their mind and enjoy the freedoms that we take for granted in this country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gerry Weiner (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-U.S.S.R.-EMIGRATION OF JEWS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is such support as this that gives strength to the Jewish people in the Soviet Union. We cannot let them be forgotten because that is just what the Soviet Union would hope for. The Member, his confreres on the committee and the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations (Mr. Kilgour) have always shown that same dedication to care and concern.
I wish I could give a more positive report, but the Government is closely monitoring developments in the Soviet Union and recognizes that there are some signs of positive movement

November 19, 1985
Adjournment Debate
on the human rights front in general, and in Soviet Jewry in particular. These, however, remain to be confirmed. Indeed, speculation continues that Jewish emigration from the Soviet Union may be on the way up.
While emigration statistics do not support the notion of an easing in the situation of Soviet Jews-130 exit visas were issued in October-there are unconfirmed reports that a number of prominent refusniks may be released after the Geneva meeting between U.S. President Reagan and Soviet Secretary General Gorbachev.
Canada has repeatedly urged the Soviet Union to adhere to internationally recognized fundamental human rights which include freedom of religion, cultural expression and emigration. We would welcome any and all indications that Soviet authorities are beginning to re-examine their policy on these matters.
For its part, the Government is involved in various initiatives to impress upon the Soviets the importance and positive ramifications of an improvement in their human rights record. Most recently, for example, senior Canadian officials have made representations in Moscow and in Ottawa on family reunification cases. In addition, officials have stressed to Soviet authorities the constraints on popular support and confidence in our bilateral relations which the Soviet human rights performance and its policy toward Soviet Jews generate.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, the Government would commend all positive developments relating to Soviet Jewry and would welcome a Soviet decision to permit increased Jewish emigration.

subtopic: CANADIAN SOVEREIGNTY-FLIGHT OVER POLAR SEA IN CANADIAN WATERS. (B) DROPPING OF CANADIAN FLAG ON UNITED STATES VESSEL
CANADIAN SOVEREIGNTY-FLIGHT OVER POLAR SEA IN CANADIAN WATERS. (B) DROPPING OF CANADIAN FLAG ON UNITED STATES VESSEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 29 I raised a question of great concern to Canadians involving the repercussions from the incursion of the Polar Sea icebreaker in Canadian waters in the Arctic earlier this summer. I want to deal with the issue broadly rather than just with the very particular issue of the investigation of the pilot of the Twin Otter who dropped a Canadian flag on our behalf on the Polar Sea and claimed Canadian sovereignty of these waters.
The facts are that the United States Coastguard icebreaker, the Polar Sea, entered Canadian waters in the summer, making this trip without asking the permission of the Canadian Government. Our Government, in a way very humiliating to Canadians, responded by offering permission, when it was not even asked for, demonstrating throughout a thorough incompetence in not understanding the seriousness of the matter.
When I raised this issue on October 29 the Government acknowledged the fact of an investigation of the pilot concerned, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) blamed former Liberal Governments for their failure to provide adequately for Canadian sovereignty in the north, certainly a
cop-out if ever there were one. The present Conservative Government was amply warned of the seriousness of the situation by Canadians, members of the Opposition and by Inuit who, of course, are very intimately concerned with sovereignty of our Arctic waters. The Conservative Government discounted all these concerns.
When the Government failed to act, Canadians acted for themselves. 1 am proud to say that the Council of Canadians organized an expedition to claim Canadian sovereignty on behalf of Canadians and, on August 8, dropped a canister from a Twin Otter. The canister contained a Canadian flag and messages claiming Canadian sovereignty, asking the United States ice-breaker to go back. Canadians then went on to another island, Princess Royal Island, and planted Canadian flags there, again to demonstrate Canadian concerns in the Arctic.
No harm was done either to persons or property. This was an important symbolic gesture that was made for all Canadians. These people represented us there when our Government failed to act responsibly.
Let me point out that this was not even a hostile act in any ordinary sense of the term. Canadians, certainly the Council of Canadians, do not want hostile relations with the United States, but friendly relations between mature nations as equals and people who consider each other's needs, and respect each other's interests and rights. When the Government simply agrees with another nations and allows it to do what it wants, being reluctant to assert what is clearly our rights, is not being friendly, but undignified and irresponsible to other Canadians.
A positive result from this incident is that the Government was forced to think about this position and take action. I welcome the statement made in the House by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) on September 10 that in the future Canada will exercise full sovereignty in northern waters and islands. This is not to say that the measures which were proposed are the best measures possible, i would certainly advocate discussion with northern peoples because the Northwest Territories Council is concerned about some of the measures that were proposed.
The commissioning of an ice-breaker, the plan for increased surveillance and the removal of a bar on appeals to the World Court are positive measures. Canada will now permit an appeal to the World Court and I believe that will clearly demonstrate that our claim to sovereignty is a most reasonable claim and recognized in international law.
Negative measures, such as an investigation of the pilot concerned, are reprehensible. The Government is taking a petty step in possibly punishing the pilot for making a harmless but important symbolic gesture on behalf of us all. The Inuit people are most concerned, as is the Council of Canadians and other Canadians.
I repeat the suggestion I made on October 29, that the people who represented us in the Arctic waters and made this symbolic gesture deserve our appreciation. Rather than con-
November 19, 1985

duct a further investigation against them, they should be awarded medals.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gerry Weiner (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN SOVEREIGNTY-FLIGHT OVER POLAR SEA IN CANADIAN WATERS. (B) DROPPING OF CANADIAN FLAG ON UNITED STATES VESSEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as Hon. Members of the House know from having passed the amendments to the Aeronautics Act, Bill C-36, earlier this summer, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) has a statutory responsibility to supervise all matters connected with aeronautics. Part of that mandate includes ensuring that operators are in compliance with air safety regulations. On August 8, 1985, the Department received a complaint that an aircraft had made two low passes over the Polar Sea. Two objects were dropped from the aircraft, one of which landed on the ship.
It has been the Department's experience, in over 40 years of concern with flight safety, that unauthorized low flying presents a great hazard to persons both in the aircraft and on the ground. Furthermore, the risk created to persons and property on this ship by the dropping of a canister weighing several pounds at flying speed clearly required a thorough investigation. The applicability of Air Regulation 508 which the Minister quoted in the House on November 1 may relate directly to this incident. The investigation is now nearing completion.
As a routine procedure in such administrative cases, both the pilot who flew the aircraft and the co-pilot who dropped the object have been issued allegation letters seeking their explanation of their involvement in this incident. These explanations were to be submitted by November 19, 1985. The pilot has responded, the co-pilot has been granted an extension to November 23, 1985.
In keeping with Departmental guidelines that are available to the public, the facts presented by both the investigator and the two pilots will be reviewed by a third party. If no violation is found, no sanction will be imposed. However, if a violation is found, then administrative sanctions will be imposed commensurate with the nature and gravity of the offence.
Hon. Members of this House will certainly appreciate that while the matter is outstanding it is not appropriate for me to comment further; until a final decision is taken by the Minister in this matter.

subtopic: SMALL BUSINESS-COMPATIBILITY OF FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL INVESTMENT ADVANTAGES
SMALL BUSINESS-COMPATIBILITY OF FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL INVESTMENT ADVANTAGES
speechtext:
On November 5, Mr. Speaker, I asked the Minister of Finance whether he had the intention of granting tax incentives to the Small Business Investment Corporations and the Societes de placement dans Ventreprise quebecoise-SPEQs for short. I asked him whether it was his intention to provide some incentives for Quebec investors and to grant them comparable tax benefits if they bought shares through the SPEQs program. In his reply the
Adjournment Debate
Minister did mention incentives with respect to small business investment corporations but did not refer to SPEQs. That is why I want to clarify my question today in an attempt to elicit a more formal explanation from the Minister.
As you know, in its April 23, 1985 Budget the Government of Quebec announced the creation of SPEQs and unveiled regulations governing them. The purpose of the program is to promote investments of risk capital in private corporations known to be small- and medium-sized businesses. Quebec residents who should decide to invest in these SPEQs will be given generous tax incentives.
The general goals of the SPEQs are as follows: to increase the shareholders' equity capital in the financial structure of Quebec small and medium-sized businesses; to encourage the shareholders of small and medium-sized businesses to invest more in their own businesses; to make it possible for those shareholders to involve other investors in the financing of their businesses; and, finally, to make it easier for small and medium-sized businesses to get started and to expand.
In order to further increase the funding opportunities of small and medium-sized businesses, the Quebec government, through its Industrial Development Corporation, decided to set up as well a capitalization loan program involving a loan granted by a private financial institution and fully guaranteed by the Quebec Industrial Development Corporation for a maximum of 10 years.
The CAPI or capitalization loan is so called because it is designed to encourage the capitalization of the recipient business. The QIDC subject to regulations will agree to guarantee this business capitalization loan for an amount equivalent to the subscribed capital by a Quebec business investment corporation in a small and medium-sized business in Quebec. The Quebec Government will thus be doubling the equity capital of Quebec investors in small and medium-sized businesses. Moreover, in addition to guaranteeing the capital, the Quebec Government will reimburse the borrowing business for the interest paid which, however, should not exceed the preferential rate plus 1 per cent. For the first two years of the loan, 100 per cent of the interest will be reimbursed, and 50 per cent for the next three years.
This is an important incentive for our businesses, and what I want to know exactly is this: Since this promotes investments by Quebecers and reduces their cost by 25 per cent, will the Federal Minister of Finance, in view of the timeliness and relevance of this method of financing Quebec businesses, allow Quebecers who invest in SPEQ's to deduct the amounts invested not only from their provincial taxable income, but also from their federal taxable income? That is my question. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

speakeroldname: Mr. John McDermid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: SMALL BUSINESS-COMPATIBILITY OF FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL INVESTMENT ADVANTAGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise this evening to reply to the question asked by the Hon. Member for

November 19, 1985
Adjournment Debate
Levis (Mr. Fontaine) about the small business investment proposals announced by the Government in its Budget last May 23. The question of the Hon. Member concerns the compatibitily of the federal proposals and the tax incentives for small businesses recently announced by the Quebec Government.
The factors relevant to this matter are complex. I would like briefly to provide some background information before addressing the specific question of the Hon. Member.
As he knows, the tax measures to stimulate small business investments introduced by the federal Government in the May Budget are quite extensive. For example, measures were introduced to expand the list of qualifying investments for deferred income plans, such as RRSPs, to include securities issued by smaller Canadian businesses. Important incentives were also introduced to encourage pension and other deferred plans to undertake these investments. Furthermore, the federal proposals provide for a number of tax measures to facilitate the channelling of such funds to small business. These include the creation of special partnership, trust and corporate fund pooling vehicles which will receive certain preferential tax treatment.
The Hon. Member's question refers to one of these pooling vehicles, the small business investment corporation or SBIC. I would point out that the SBIC is a special type of non-taxable corporation designed exclusively for pension funds to assist them in making their small business investments. I think, therefore, that the Hon. Member's question is really about the more general relationship between the federal Government and the Quebec Government, in particular, whether investors in Quebec SPEQs, or Societe de placements dans I'entreprise quebecoise, will also qualify under the provisions of the federal small business legislation.
This by no means is a simple matter. Its various ramifications are currently being explored by both the federal and Quebec Governments. In this regard, the federal Government has recently received a formal request from the Government of Quebec. I can tell the Hon. Member that the feedback to date has been impressive. All indications are that there will be a substantial increase in available small business financing as a result of the measures being discussed. We are actively exploring ways in which federal and provincial efforts can be coordinated to enhance further the effect of the measures.
